newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court to decide third-party debate case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court to decide third-party debate case.

text.p: The Supreme Court said Monday it would decide a free-speech case on whether a third-party congressional candidate may be barred from a debate on the state's public television network.

The justices agreed to review an appeals court ruling that a governmentally owned and controlled television station must include in a debate it stages any candidate who is legally qualified to appear on the ballot under state law.
The high court will hear arguments in the case during its term that begins in October, with a decision likely next year.
The case involved Ralph Forbes, who ran in 1992 as an independent, third-party candidate for a seat in Congress from Arkansas.

The Arkansas Educational Television Network, with five public television stations, excluded him from a debate it sponsored because he was not a politically viable candidate. The Democratic and Republican candidates participated.
Forbes sued, saying the reason for his exclusion was not sufficient under First Amendment, free-speech protections.
A U.S. appeals court ruled for Forbes, holding that a debate between political candidates organised anbd broadcast by a state public television network was a limited public forum.

The state public television network replied that the First Amendment protects its editorial judgments that are free from political interference and that apply rational, neutral policies in making journalistic decisions about the debate.
Lawyers for the association representing public television stations nationwide and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting supported the state network.
They said the appeals court's decision "will restrict the ability of public television stations to provide campaign coverage, undermining the core purpose of the First Amendment."
The Justice Department and the Federal Communications Commission also supported the state public television network.
"This court...should preserve the editoral discretion that state-entity licensees have traditionally exercised over the content of their news programming," the two agencies said.

The case was unrelated to the lawsuit filed by third-party presidential candidate Ross Perot over his exclusion from last year's debates. Perot unsuccessfully sued the Federal Election Commission and a bipartisan commission which set up the debate.
In other action, the Supreme Court agreed to hear an appeal by Louisiana defending its so-called "open elections system" for congressional races.

The system, in effect nearly 20 years, allows for a primary in October in which all candidates appear on the same ballot and all voters may vote. A candidate who runs unopposed or who receives a majority of the votes is elected.

The names of congressional candidates appear on the general election ballot only if no single candidate gets a majority of votes in the primary and a runoff is required between the two top candidates.
Since 1978, more than 80 percent of the contested congressional elections have been decided in the state's October primary.
Four voters sued, claiming the system violated the constitutional requirement for a federal election day in November.
